lead: A petrol engine needs a spark across the plug gap a little before the end of compression, and the gap needs roughly 10–20 kV to break down. The battery-and-coil ignition system makes that spark from a 12 V battery. Current builds in a low-voltage primary winding, a contact breaker opens the circuit, and the collapsing magnetic field induces a high voltage in a secondary winding. A distributor sends the pulse to the right cylinder. It is also called the Kettering system or contact-point ignition.
prereq: You need: the battery, ignition switch and wiring of the vehicle power supply, and the idea that a changing current makes a changing magnetic field.

blocks.text: An ignition system has four jobs: make a voltage high enough to jump the plug gap; send it to the cylinder that is ready; fire at the right crank angle, a little before top dead centre (TDC), because the flame takes time to build pressure; and move that angle with speed and load.

The battery-and-coil system does all four. A 12 V battery, the ignition switch and a ballast resistor feed the coil's primary winding. It limits the running current and is bypassed during cranking, when the starter pulls the battery down to about 9–10 V. A cam-driven contact breaker (the points) completes the primary circuit to earth. A secondary winding sits on the same iron core. A distributor with a rotor and cap routes the secondary pulse to each plug in the firing order, and each plug returns the current to earth through the engine block.

sections.h3: How the collapse makes high voltage

blocks.text: When the points close, current builds in the primary winding, a few hundred turns of thick wire, and sets up a magnetic field in the iron core. At the firing point a cam lobe opens the points, the current falls to zero and the field collapses. A changing flux Φ induces an emf in every turn:

blocks.where: e is the induced emf in volts (V), N the number of turns, Φ the magnetic flux in webers (Wb) and t the time in seconds (s). The minus sign is Lenz's law: the emf opposes the change.

blocks.text: The same core links both windings, so the collapse induces an emf in both. This is mutual induction. The primary emf at the break is a few hundred volts; the secondary has many thousands of turns of fine wire, about 100 times the primary turns, so its emf is roughly e₂ = (N₂/N₁) × e₁, which is 10 kV or more. The speed of the collapse matters as much as the turns ratio: a fast fall gives a large dΦ/dt.

sections.h3: Dwell, coil current and the capacitor

blocks.text: Dwell is the period for which the points stay closed and current flows in the primary. The dwell angle is the angle the cam turns in that period; data books quote it in distributor (cam) degrees or crank degrees. On a four-stroke engine the cam turns at half engine speed, so one cam degree is two crank degrees. A four-stroke engine of z cylinders sparks once every 720°/z of crank, and the time between sparks is:

blocks.where: T<sub>s</sub> is the spark interval in seconds, N the engine speed in rev/min and z the number of cylinders. If the points are closed for a fraction D of each interval, the dwell angle is θ<sub>d</sub> = D × 720°/z crank degrees and the dwell time is t<sub>d</sub> = D × T<sub>s</sub>.

blocks.text: The coil current does not jump to its full value. The primary has inductance L and resistance R, so the current rises along a curve:

blocks.where: i is the primary current in amperes after the points have been closed for t seconds, V the supply voltage, R the total primary resistance in ohms, L the primary inductance in henries and τ the time constant in seconds. The energy stored at the break is E = ½ L i².

blocks.text: With points the dwell angle is fixed by the cam, so at high speed the dwell time shrinks and the spark weakens (worked example 2).

A capacitor of about 0.2–0.3 µF, often called the condenser, sits across the points. Without it the current would arc across the opening points, burning them and slowing the collapse. The capacitor takes the current for the first instant, so the points open cleanly, the current falls fast, and the secondary voltage is high.

The flame takes roughly the same time to burn, while the piston moves faster as speed rises, so the spark must come earlier at high speed. A thin, diluted part-load charge burns slowly and also needs more advance; at full load the dense charge burns faster, and too much advance causes knock.

Centrifugal advance uses two weights on a plate driven by the distributor shaft. As speed rises the weights swing out against springs and turn the cam ahead of the shaft, so the points open earlier. Vacuum advance uses a diaphragm fed from a small port just above the closed throttle plate. At idle the port sees almost no vacuum; at part-throttle cruise it sees high vacuum and the diaphragm turns the breaker plate against the cam rotation, adding advance. At full throttle the vacuum is low and a spring removes that advance.

Base (static) timing is set at idle with the vacuum pipe disconnected and plugged, using a timing light on the pulley marks. Total advance = base + centrifugal + vacuum. The ECU of electronic and programmed ignition replaces both with a stored map.

examples.question: A four-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 3000 rpm. The contact-breaker dwell is 60% of the spark interval. Find the spark frequency, the spark interval, the dwell angle in crank and cam degrees, and the dwell time.
steps: A four-stroke cycle is 720° of crank and four cylinders fire once each per cycle, so one spark every 720°/4 = 180° of crank, two sparks per revolution.
Spark interval T<sub>s</sub> = 120 ÷ (3000 × 4) = 0.010 s = 10 ms (the same as 1/f).
Dwell angle = 0.60 × 180° = 108° of crank. The cam turns at half speed, so this is 108/2 = 54° of cam.
examples.answer: Spark frequency 100 sparks/s; spark interval 10 ms; dwell angle 108° of crank (54° of cam); dwell time 6 ms.

examples.question: The same engine's coil has primary inductance L = 8 mH, and the coil with its ballast resistor has R = 3.0 Ω on a 12 V supply. Find the current at the break and the energy stored at 3000 rpm (dwell time 6 ms) and at 6000 rpm, where the same 60% dwell lasts only 3 ms.
steps: Final current V/R = 12 ÷ 3.0 = 4.0 A. Time constant τ = L/R = 0.008 ÷ 3.0 = 2.67 ms.
Ratio 29.2 ÷ 51.2 = 0.57: doubling the speed leaves only 57% of the spark energy, because the fixed dwell angle now lasts half the time.
examples.answer: 3.58 A and 51.2 mJ at 3000 rpm; 2.70 A and 29.2 mJ at 6000 rpm, a 43% loss of spark energy.

traps: Using rpm/60 as the spark frequency and forgetting the ×2 for a four-cylinder four-stroke engine.
Taking 60% of 360° instead of 60% of the angle between two sparks (180° of crank here), or mixing cam degrees with crank degrees.
Saying the capacitor adds spark energy. It stops the points arcing, which makes the collapse fast.
Taking vacuum advance from the manifold below the throttle. The port sits just above the throttle plate, so there is almost no vacuum advance at idle.

quiz.q: Define dwell angle and dwell time.
quiz.a: Dwell angle is the cam (or crank) angle during which the points stay closed. Dwell time is the same closed period in seconds.

quiz.q: Why does the secondary high voltage appear when the points open, not while they are closed?
quiz.a: While the points are closed the current settles to a steady value, so the flux is steady and dΦ/dt is zero. Opening the points collapses the flux quickly, and the fast change induces a large emf in the many secondary turns.

quiz.q: Why is a capacitor connected across the contact-breaker points?
quiz.a: It takes the primary current for the first instant as the points open, so no arc forms. The current then falls quickly, the flux collapses fast and the secondary voltage is high. It also stops the points burning.

quiz.q: A six-cylinder, four-stroke engine runs at 2400 rpm with dwell equal to 55% of the spark interval. Find the spark frequency, spark interval, dwell angle in crank degrees and dwell time.
quiz.a: 2400 rpm = 40 rev/s; six cylinders give 3 sparks per revolution, so f = 120 sparks/s. T<sub>s</sub> = 1/120 = 8.33 ms. Spark angle = 720°/6 = 120° of crank. Dwell angle = 0.55 × 120° = 66° of crank. Dwell time = 0.55 × 8.33 ms = 4.58 ms.

quiz.q: On a contact-point system the dwell angle is fixed. Explain what happens to the dwell time and the spark as the speed rises.
quiz.a: The same angle passes in less time, so the dwell time falls. The primary current has less time to rise along its i = (V/R)(1 − e<sup>−t/τ</sup>) curve, so the stored energy ½Li² and the secondary voltage fall. In worked example 2 the energy drops from 51.2 mJ to 29.2 mJ when the speed doubles.

beyond: Capacitor discharge ignition, used on racing and many small two-wheeler engines, stores energy in a capacitor at a few hundred volts for a very fast voltage rise. Search terms: Kettering ignition, dwell control, capacitor discharge ignition.
